content: Burdock is a group of biennial thistles belonging to the genus Arctium in the family Asteraceae. The species Arctium minus, commonly known as Common Burdock, is found growing wild across North America, Europe, and Asia. Plants in the Arctium genus have dark green leaves that can reach up to 18 inches (45 cm) in length. These leaves are typically large, coarse, and ovate, with the lower leaves being heart-shaped. The underside of the leaves is woolly, and the leaf stalks are generally hollow. Arctium species typically flower between July and October. The prickly seed heads of these plants are known for their ability to easily attach to fur and clothing, which aids in seed dispersal. However, these burrs can cause local irritation and may lead to intestinal hairballs in pets, though most animals tend to avoid consuming these plants. Historically, many species were classified under the genus Arctium, but most have since been reclassified into the related genus Cousinia. The distinction between Arctium and Cousinia is not always clear, as their molecular phylogeny is closely related. Burdock is sometimes confused with cockleburs (Xanthium genus) and rhubarb (Rheum genus). The roots of burdock serve as a food source for the larvae of the Ghost Moth (Hepialus humuli), and the plant is also utilized by other Lepidoptera species, such as the Brown-tail, Coleophora paripennella, Coleophora peribenanderi, the Gothic, Lime-speck Pug, and Scalloped Hazel. The green, above-ground parts of the plant can cause contact dermatitis in humans due to the lactones it produces. Uses Food and Drink The taproot of young burdock plants can be harvested and consumed as a root vegetable. While it is not commonly used in modern European cuisine, it remains popular in Asia, particularly in Japan, where Arctium lappa (Greater Burdock) is known as gobō (牛蒡 or ゴボウ). Cultivated burdock plants produce slender roots that can grow up to 1 meter long and 2 cm in diameter. The root is crisp and has a sweet, mild, and slightly pungent flavor, with a hint of earthy harshness that can be reduced by soaking julienned or shredded roots in water for 5–10 minutes. Immature flower stalks can also be harvested in late spring before the flowers bloom, and their taste is similar to artichoke, a related plant. A popular Japanese dish, kinpira gobō, consists of julienned or shredded burdock root and carrot braised with soy sauce, sugar, mirin, sake, and sesame oil. Another dish is burdock makizushi, sushi filled with pickled burdock root, which is often artificially colored orange to resemble a carrot. In the latter half of the 20th century, burdock gained international recognition for its culinary uses due to the growing popularity of the macrobiotic diet, which advocates its consumption. Burdock root is a good source of dietary fiber (6 g per 100 g), calcium, potassium, and amino acids, while being low in calories. It also contains polyphenols, which can cause surface darkening and earthy harshness due to the formation of tannin-iron complexes. However, this flavor profile pairs well with pork in miso soup (tonjiru) and Japanese-style pilaf (takikomi gohan). In the United Kingdom, a soft drink called dandelion and burdock has been popular for many years. Burdock is also believed to act as a galactagogue, a substance that promotes lactation. Traditional Medicine In folk herbal medicine, dried burdock is considered a diuretic, diaphoretic, and blood-purifying agent. The seeds of Arctium lappa are used in traditional Chinese medicine under the name niupangzi (牛蒡子). Burdock has been traditionally used as a medicinal herb for various ailments. Burdock root oil extract, also known as bur oil, is popular in Europe as a scalp treatment. It is applied to improve hair strength, shine, and body, as well as to address scalp conditions such as dandruff and combat hair loss. Modern studies suggest that burdock root oil extract is rich in phytosterols and essential fatty acids, including rare long-chain EFAs, which are essential for maintaining a healthy scalp and promoting natural hair growth. The oil provides immediate relief while supporting the normal functions of sebaceous glands and hair follicles. Some European herbalists recommend combining burdock root oil with nettle root oil and massaging the mixture into the scalp daily for enhanced effects. Burdock and Velcro In the early 1940s, Swiss inventor George de Mestral became intrigued by the burdock seeds that clung to his clothes and his dog’s fur during a walk. Upon examining the seeds under a microscope, he observed their hook-and-loop mechanism, which allows them to attach to passing animals for seed dispersal. This observation inspired him to create Velcro. Tolstoy The Russian writer Leo Tolstoy mentioned burdock in his journal in 1896. He described seeing a small burdock shoot in a plowed field, black from dust but still alive and red in the center, which inspired him to write. Species Arctium lappa: Greater Burdock, Gobō Arctium minus: Lesser Burdock, Burweed, Louse-bur, Button-bur Arctium minus nemorosum (syn. Arctium vulgare): Woodland Burdock, Wood Burdock Arctium pubens: Common Burdock Arctium tomentosum: Downy Burdock, Woolly Burdock Safety The roots of burdock closely resemble those of Deadly Nightshade (Atropa belladonna), also known as belladonna, which is a highly toxic plant. This similarity poses a risk of contamination in burdock preparations. It is essential to purchase products from reputable companies and avoid gathering burdock in the wild unless you are confident in your ability to correctly identify the plant.
